questions.q: What does a Schema Registry actually store and enforce, per this lesson?
options: Every version of every topic's schema, enforcing compatibility rules before a new version is accepted
The full contents of every message ever produced to every topic
Only consumer group offsets, not schema information
A single global schema shared by every topic in the cluster
questions.explain: The Registry is a central, versioned store of schemas with compatibility enforcement — not a message store.

questions.q: What does BACKWARD compatibility mean, as defined in this lesson?
options: A new schema can read data written with the old schema, making it safe to upgrade consumers first
An old schema can read data written with a new schema
Schemas can never be changed once registered
Only the most recent schema version is ever usable
questions.explain: Backward compatibility specifically protects the direction of upgrading consumers before producers.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which side(s) of a Kafka pipeline actually check against the Schema Registry?
options: Both the producer, before sending, and the consumer, when deserializing — not just one side
Only the producer; consumers never interact with the Registry
Only the consumer; producers never interact with the Registry
Neither side checks — the broker enforces schemas independently
questions.explain: Producers check schema validity before sending, and consumers fetch the exact registered version to deserialize correctly.

questions.q: Why does a consumer fetch a specific schema version rather than always assuming the latest one, per this lesson?
options: Because a message might have been written with an older, still-valid schema version, and the consumer needs the version it was actually written with
Because the Registry only stores the single most recent schema version at any time
Because consumers are not allowed to read messages older than the newest schema
Schema version has no effect on how a message is deserialized
questions.explain: The schema ID is embedded in the message, so the consumer deserializes using the schema version that message was actually written with.
